🚨 🇺🇸 The US is now paying more than $1.05 trillion in interest on its debt every year even as the economy continues to perform relatively well.

📊 In fiscal 2026, net interest payments on federal debt reached $1.05 trillion, up from $970 billion in 2025. Nearly 20% of federal revenue now goes exclusively toward paying creditors⚠️. Meanwhile, the federal deficit is approaching $2 trillion (roughly 6.2% of GDP) while gross federal debt has surpassed $40 trillion. We're talking about a country running enormous deficits despite not being in a major recession.

📈 Over the past five years, the average interest rate paid on marketable Treasury securities has risen from 1.47% to 3.52% while 10-year Treasury yields are now hovering around 5%. This is particularly problematic because the US must continuously refinance its outstanding debt as bonds mature. Debt issued several years ago at 1.5% may now need to be replaced with new borrowing at 4% or 5%. The process is gradual but even without an acceleration in government spending, interest costs could continue rising for years.

⚠️ However, debt sustainability also depends on nominal economic growth. When nominal GDP grows faster than the effective interest rate, growth helps reduce the debt burden relative to GDP, all else being equal. In Q2 2026, US nominal GDP was still growing by 6.3% year over year, compared with an average interest cost of 3.52% on marketable debt at the end of September. That's one reason why I don't believe a fiscal crisis is imminent but the US is also running a primary deficit of nearly $940 billion, meaning a deficit before even accounting for interest payments. The US continues to spend significantly more than it collects, even before servicing its debt.

➡️ The Trump administration is placing considerable faith in AI to improve this equation through productivity gains. I find that optimism risky, as investing hundreds of billions of dollars in data centers does not guarantee enough additional growth or tax revenue to stabilize the debt. The Congressional Budget Office projected in February that federal debt held by the public would reach 120% of GDP by 2036, while annual net interest payments could exceed $2 trillion. This situation could also keep long-term bond yields elevated even if the Fed gradually cuts short-term interest rates.
